title: The First Americans
objective: After this level you can explain how people first reached the Americas from Asia during the last Ice Age, and why the timing is still debated.
summary: Ice Age seas exposed Beringia, and people crossed from East Asia, perhaps also by boat along the coast. Clovis was long thought first; Monte Verde proved otherwise, and White Sands is still debated.

cards.headline: The first Americans didn’t need a ship. They may have walked.
cards.body: During the last Ice Age, Asia and Alaska were joined by dry land. How did people get here, and when? The first answer is fairly settled. The second is still an argument.

cards.headline: A bridge made by the Ice Age
cards.body: So much of Earth’s water was frozen in glaciers that sea levels fell by as much as about 400 feet. That exposed Beringia, dry land linking Siberia and Alaska where the Bering Strait’s seafloor is now. Many scientists think people crossed from East Asia this way, following the animals they hunted. Others propose that some came by boat, along the coast. Either way, nobody set out to discover a continent. They were after dinner.

cards.headline: The Clovis-first idea
cards.body: Archaeologists kept finding one beautiful tool: a leaf-shaped, fluted stone spear point, the mark of the Clovis culture. For decades, Clovis artifacts, about 13,000 years old, were the oldest known in the Americas. So many archaeologists concluded that the Clovis people were the first Americans. It was a tidy story. Then came Chile.

cards.headline: Older than Clovis
cards.body: At Monte Verde, a campsite in southern Chile, people were living more than 14,000 years ago, earlier than Clovis and a very long walk from Alaska. Archaeologists broadly accepted the site’s early date in 1997, and the Clovis-first idea fell. Now human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, dated to about 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, push the story back further. Some archaeologists remain skeptical of those dates. Stay tuned.

mascot.line: Keep the two questions apart: the route is fairly settled; the date is the argument.

cards.headline: The first Americans: route and date
learned: Ice Age seas exposed Beringia, linking Siberia and Alaska
Many think people crossed from East Asia; some came by boat
Monte Verde (accepted 1997) is older than Clovis
The White Sands footprints may be 21,000 to 23,000 years old

questions.prompt: What was Beringia during the last Ice Age?

options.label: A huge glacier that covered all of North America
options.rationale: It was land exposed when the seas fell.

options.label: An Ice Age campsite in southern Chile
Dry land linking Siberia and Alaska
A sea route from Europe to eastern Canada
options.rationale: It linked Asia, not Europe, to Alaska.

questions.explanation: Low Ice Age seas exposed Beringia, dry land linking Siberia and Alaska.

questions.prompt: Why did Monte Verde overturn the Clovis-first idea?

options.label: People lived there before the Clovis culture
It held the oldest Clovis spear points ever found
options.rationale: Its people were earlier than Clovis.

options.label: It proved people came from Europe, not Asia
options.rationale: It changed the date, not the direction.

options.label: It showed that Beringia was never dry land

questions.explanation: People lived at Monte Verde more than 14,000 years ago, earlier than Clovis (about 13,000).

questions.prompt: Level 1 dated the first Americans to about 25,000 to 15,000 years ago. Which find sits near the older end of that range?

options.label: The Monte Verde campsite
options.rationale: It is more than 14,000 years old, not over 20,000.

options.label: The Bering Land Bridge
options.rationale: That’s a route, not a dated find.

questions.explanation: The White Sands footprints are dated to about 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, though some archaeologists doubt it.
